claims.text: Actively learned moment tensor potentials coupled to an analytical free-energy model can reliably compute fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties.
The proposed method explicitly retains vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
The proposed method costs only a fraction as much as explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD.
Actively learned moment tensor potentials parameterized with ab initio data have been demonstrated in refractory multi-principal-element-alloy studies.
The demonstrated refractory-alloy framework combined actively learned moment tensor potentials with an analytical model.
Replacing explicit molecular-dynamics free-energy evaluation with the proposed potential-plus-analytical-model workflow will reduce computational expense.
The method is applicable at approximately 0.9–1.1 times the melting temperature.
The method is applicable from elemental and binary systems through multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Moment tensor potentials can capture local bonding and anharmonic vibrational behavior relevant to fusion.
Moment tensor potentials can capture the effects of electron–vibration interactions.
Moment tensor potentials emulate the ab initio potential-energy surface with high fidelity.
Using moment tensor potentials produces a dramatic reduction in computational cost.
Coupling the potentials to an analytical model prevents loss of essential entropy contributions and therefore maintains accurate solid- and liquid-phase free energies.
Fusion free energies and related observables will agree with explicit ab initio molecular dynamics to within approximately 5%.
The proposed workflow will be at least ten times faster than both TOR-TILD and explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
Traditional explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics and TOR-TILD workflows compute free energies directly.
The approach is expected to work near phase-transition temperatures in elemental, binary, and complex multicomponent high-entropy systems.
Actively learned moment tensor potentials have shown promise for optimizing mechanical properties in refractory multi-principal-element alloys.
Actively learned moment tensor potentials have shown promise for free-energy calculations in simpler elemental or binary systems.
The quantitative accuracy of the proposed method for fusion properties across diverse multicomponent systems has not been established.
